prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?

If the font you named isn’t available, the browser falls back to its generic default (usually “sans‑serif”), which is why you see a “generic” look. | **No `glyphs` URL** (offline) | Omit the `glyphs` field *or* point it at a dummy URL (e.g. `""`). Native will ignore it if `font-faces` is present. |
| **Use device‑bundled fonts** | Add the font files (TTF/OTF) to your app’s `assets/` (or `res/raw/`) and reference them in a `font-faces` array in the style JSON. |
| **Map each `text-font` name to a concrete file + Unicode range** | In `font-faces` you give a **font‑family name** (the same string you use in `text-font`) and a **list of local files** together with the **code‑point ranges** that each file covers. |
| **Support non‑Latin scripts** | Add the appropriate Noto (or any other) script fonts to the bundle and list their ranges. CJK is special – you must supply the ranges yourself (or accept the default on‑device TinySDF fallback, which Native does **not** do automatically). |
| **RTL (Arabic, Hebrew, etc.)** | Load the RTL text plugin **only for GL JS** – Native does not need a plugin; you just need the correct font and the Unicode ranges. |
| **Shaping‑heavy scripts (Devanagari, Khmer, etc.)** | Native cannot shape them (no HarfBuzz). Even with the right font they will look broken. The only workaround today is to avoid those scripts or pre‑rasterise the labels into icons. |

Description: negative — out-of-scope question about hillshade/terrain layers
prompt: How do I add a hillshade layer from a raster-dem source to my MapLibre GL JS style?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a complete, copy‑and‑paste‑ready guide that shows **how to add a hillshade layer** that is driven by a **raster‑DEM source** to a MapLibre GL JS map. It covers everything you need to know: | Step | What you do | Why it matters | |------|-------------|----------------| | 1️⃣ | Choose a DEM tile service (or host your own) | The hillshade layer reads elevation values from a `raster‑dem` source. | | 2️⃣ | Add the DEM as a `raster-dem` source | This tells MapLibre that the tiles contain elevation data, not ordinary imagery. | | 3️⃣ | Add a `hillshade` layer that points at that source | The layer does the actual shading work (light direction, exaggeration, etc.). | | 4️⃣ | (Optional) Add a `terrain` source if you also want 3‑D terrain | Hillshade works without it, but you often want both. | | 5️⃣ | Tune the hillshade paint properties to get the look you want | Exaggeration, illumination direction, shadow/ highlight colours, etc. | | 6️⃣ | Handle CORS / token requirements | DEM tiles are often behind a token or need CORS headers. | --- ## 1️⃣ Pick a DEM source You can use any raster‑DEM that serves 16‑bit PNG (or WebP) tiles. Here are a few ready‑made options (all free for low‑volume use): | Provider | URL template | Notes | |----------|--------------|-------| | **MapTiler DEM** | `https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/terrain-rgb/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=YOUR_KEY` | 16‑bit “terrain‑rgb” tiles (same format Mapbox uses). | | **OpenMapTiles DEM** | `https://tiles.openmaptiles.org/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Public demo server (rate‑limited). | | **Your own tiles** | `https://mydomain.com/tiles/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Must be CORS‑enabled and serve 16‑bit PNG. | > **Tip:** If you only need a quick demo, the MapTiler URL works out‑of‑the‑box – just replace `YOUR_KEY` with a free API key from . --- ## 2️⃣ Add the DEM as a `raster-dem` source ```js map.addSource('dem', { type: 'raster-dem', // The URL must contain {z}/{x}/{y} placeholders. url: 'https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/terrain-rgb/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=YOUR_KEY', tileSize: 256, // most DEM tiles are 256 px maxzoom: 14, // highest zoom you have tiles for attribution: '© MapTiler' }); ``` *Why `raster-dem`?* Only this source type tells MapLibre that the raster contains **elevation values** (encoded as 16‑bit PNG). If you used `raster` instead, the hillshade layer would see only colour data and would render nothing. --- ## 3️⃣ Add the `hillshade` layer ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'dem', // <-- the source we just added layout: {}, // hillshade has no layout properties paint: { // Optional – tweak the visual style 'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.5, // 0 = flat, 1 = real elevation 'hillshade-illumination-direction': 335, // degrees clockwise from north 'hillshade-shadow-color': 'rgba(0,0,0,0.5)', 'hillshade-highlight-color': 'rgba(255,255,255,0.5)', 'hillshade-accent-color': 'rgba(255,255,255,0.2)' } }); ``` ### What the paint properties do | Property | Typical range | Effect | |----------|---------------|--------| | `hillshade-exaggeration` | `0 … 2` (default 1) | Scales the height of the terrain for a more dramatic look. | | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | `0 … 360` (default 335) | Sun azimuth; 0 ° = north, 90 ° = east. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` | any CSS colour | Colour of the “shadowed” side of slopes. | | `hillshade-highlight-color` | any CSS colour | Colour of the “sunlit” side. | | `hillshade-accent-color` | any CSS colour | Colour of the “rim” where slopes change direction. | You can omit any of these – MapLibre will fall back to its defaults. --- ## 4️⃣ (Optional) Add a `terrain` source for 3‑D terrain If you also want the map surface to rise and fall in 3‑D (e.g. when the user tilts the map), add a `terrain` source that points at the same DEM: ```js map.setTerrain({ source: 'dem', exaggeration: 1.5 }); ``` > **Note:** The hillshade layer works **without** a terrain source. Adding terrain is purely for visual 3‑D extrusion. --- ## 5️⃣ Full minimal example (HTML) ```html MapLibre GL JS – Hillshade from raster‑DEM
``` *Replace `YOUR_KEY` with your MapTiler API key (or swap the URL for another DEM provider).* --- ## 6️⃣ Common pitfalls & how to fix them | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Hillshade layer is invisible** | • DEM source URL wrong or CORS blocked
• `type` set to `"raster"` instead of `"raster-dem"` | Open the DEM URL directly in the browser → you should see a PNG. If you get a CORS error, add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on the server or use a proxy. | | **Only flat colour, no shading** | • `hillshade-exaggeration` set to `0`
• DEM tiles contain only 0‑elevation (e.g. a placeholder) | Verify the DEM tiles contain elevation (they look like a grayscale image with subtle variation). | | **CJK text looks wrong** | Not a hillshade issue – it’s a font/glyph problem. | See the `maplibre-fonts-glyphs` skill for local‑font fallback or glyph server setup. | | **Performance drops when zoomed in** | • Using a very high `maxzoom` with low‑resolution tiles
• No tile cache | Serve DEM tiles at an appropriate maxzoom (usually 12‑14) and enable HTTP caching (`Cache‑Control`). | | **Hillshade looks too “flat”** | • `hillshade-exaggeration` too low
• Illumination direction set to a value that hides shadows | Increase `hillshade-exaggeration` (e.g. `1.5`) and experiment with `hillshade-illumination-direction`. | --- ## 7️⃣ Quick checklist before you ship - [ ] **DEM source URL** points to a tile service that returns **16‑bit PNG** (or WebP) tiles. - [ ] Source `type` is **`raster-dem`** (not `raster`). - [ ] `hillshade` layer `source` matches the DEM source ID. - [ ] Paint properties are set to values that make the shading visible at your map’s typical zoom levels. - [ ] CORS headers are present on the DEM tile server (or you’re using a same‑origin server). - [ ] If you need a token, it’s included in the URL (or you’re using a signed‑URL scheme). - [ ] (Optional) `map.setTerrain({source: 'dem', …})` is called **after** the DEM source is added. --- ## TL;DR – Minimal code snippet ```js map.addSource('dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://api.maptiler.com/tiles/terrain-rgb/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=YOUR_KEY', tileSize: 256, maxzoom: 14 }); map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'dem', paint: { 'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.7, 'hillshade-illumination-direction': 330 } }); ``` That’s it! Your map now displays a smooth, light‑shaded relief derived from the raster DEM you supplied. Happy mapping! 🚀
